title: The winner's curse
objectives: Shade a bid for a common-value prize, because winning is bad news.

screens.title: Guess the jar
screens.prose: A jar holds £V. Five bidders each estimate V with an error uniform from −£10 to +£10, and each bids the estimate. The highest bid wins. Run the auctions: each bar counts the winner's error.

state.caption: Each trial is one auction with five fresh errors.

screens.question: On average, by how much does the winning estimate overshoot V, in £?

hints.text: Run 1,000 auctions and look where the bars pile up.
Most winning errors sit between +£4 and +£10.
The mean is about £6.67.

feedback.correct: About £6.67: the winner is usually the one who guessed too high.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 auctions and estimate the centre of the bars.

byKey.zero: Each error averages 0, but the winner's is the largest of five, so it is biased up.
byKey.ten: £10 is the largest error possible. The largest of five averages less than that.

explain.text: Every estimate is unbiased, but the winning one is the largest of five. Its error averages exactly $10 \times \tfrac46 = £6.67$; 1,000 runs land near that. Winning tells you your estimate was probably too high.

screens.title: The exact overshoot
screens.prose: Rescale `puzzles` l11-largest-of-several: the largest of $n$ uniforms on 0 to 1 averages $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$. An error uniform on $-a$ to $a$ is $-a + 2aU$, with $U$ uniform on 0 to 1.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Each error is $-a + 2aU_i$, with $U_i$ uniform on 0 to 1.
The largest error is $-a + 2a \max_i U_i$, since the map keeps order.
Each error averages 0, so the winner's error averages 0.
lines.why: The winner is chosen for having the largest error. Picking the largest breaks the average of 0.

hints.text: Write one error in terms of a uniform on 0 to 1.
The largest error comes from the largest $U_i$.
Map, maximum, $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$, simplify.

feedback.correct: Map, take the largest, use $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$, simplify.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by writing one error as $-a + 2aU$.

byKey.d1: The winner is chosen for having the largest error. Picking the largest breaks the average of 0.
byKey.left-out: Every line but the one claiming the winner's error averages 0 belongs.

explain.text: The map $u \mapsto -a + 2au$ keeps order, so the largest error comes from the largest $U_i$. Its mean is $-a + 2a\tfrac{n}{n + 1} = a\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}$. With $a = 10$ and $n = 5$: £6.67.

screens.title: More bidders, bigger curse
screens.prose: Same jar, errors still ±£10, but now ten bidders each bid their estimate.
screens.question: By how much does the winner overshoot on average, in £?

hints.text: Use $a\,\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}$.

byKey.five: That is the five-bidder overshoot. With ten bidders the largest error is larger still.

explain.text: With ten bidders the overshoot is $10 \times \tfrac{9}{11} = £8.18$, approaching £10. A winner who bid her estimate loses £8.18 on average. More bidders means shading more, not less.

screens.title: Buying a firm
screens.prose: A firm is worth V to its owner, uniform from £0 to £100m. In your hands it is worth 1.6V. You make one offer b; the owner, who knows V, accepts whenever $b \ge V$.
screens.question: Put the reasoning in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: The owner accepts only when $V \le b$.
Given acceptance, V is uniform on 0 to b, so $E[V \mid \text{accept}] = b/2$.
The firm is then worth $1.6 \times b/2 = 0.8b$ to you.
Every accepted offer loses $b - 0.8b = 0.2b$ on average, so offer nothing.
The average value is £50m, worth £80m to you, so any offer below £80m pays.
lines.why: That averages over every firm. You only buy the firms worth less than your offer.

hints.text: Ask which firms you actually buy.
You buy only those with $V \le b$, which average $b/2$.
Accept, condition, value to you, loss.

feedback.correct: Condition on acceptance: every offer loses 0.2b.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from when the owner says yes.

byKey.d1: That averages over every firm. You only buy the firms worth less than your offer.
byKey.left-out: Every line but the unconditional average belongs.

explain.text: The owner says yes only when the firm is worth less than your offer. Those firms average $b/2$, worth $0.8b$ to you, so each accepted offer loses $0.2b$. The curve is below 0 for every offer above 0.

screens.title: Offer £60m?
screens.prose: A colleague says the firm averages £50m, worth £80m to us. So offer £60m and make £20m.

state.caption: The owner's value V runs from £0 to £100m.

screens.question: Is the £60m offer a good idea?

options.text: No: it loses money on average
Yes: the firm is worth £80m to us on average
options.why: You reasoned from the unconditional average. The owner accepts only when the firm is worth at most £60m.

options.text: Yes: it is accepted 60% of the time
options.why: Being accepted often is the problem. Each acceptance is a firm worth £30m to its owner on average.

hints.text: Which firms does the owner sell at £60m?
Only those worth at most £60m, which average £30m.
£30m is worth £48m to you, less than the £60m you pay.

feedback.correct: No: an accepted £60m offer buys a firm worth £48m to you.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on the owner saying yes.

byKey.b: You reasoned from the unconditional average. The owner accepts only when the firm is worth at most £60m.

explain.text: The owner sells at £60m only when the firm is worth at most £60m, £30m on average. That is worth $1.6 \times 30 = £48$m to you, so each acceptance loses £12m. The average of all firms never enters.

screens.title: What the offer costs
screens.prose: Stay with the £60m offer. It is accepted with chance 0.6, and then loses £12m.
screens.question: What is the offer's expected profit before you know the answer, in £m?

hints.text: Expected profit is the chance of acceptance times the loss when accepted.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance of acceptance by the result of an acceptance.

byKey.given: −12 is the loss once accepted. Weight it by the chance of acceptance, 0.6.
byKey.naive: That is £80m less £60m, from the unconditional average. Condition on acceptance.

explain.text: The offer is accepted with chance 0.6 and then loses £12m, so it is worth $0.6 \times (-12) = -£7.2$m. In general it is $\tfrac{b}{100}\left(\tfrac{kb}{2} - b\right)$ with $k = 1.6$. The curve at £60m reads −7.2.

screens.title: Twice the value
screens.prose: Now the firm is worth exactly twice its owner's value to you, 2V.
screens.question: What does an offer of b earn on average?

options.text: Nothing: every accepted offer breaks even

options.why: You doubled the unconditional average. Given acceptance V averages b/2, worth exactly b to you.
At twice the value the loss of the 1.6 case has shrunk to zero.

hints.text: Given acceptance, V averages b/2.
Worth $2 \times b/2 = b$ to you, the price you pay.
So every offer breaks even.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the firm's value to you given acceptance.

byKey.b: You doubled the unconditional average. Given acceptance V averages b/2, worth exactly b to you.

explain.text: At $k = 2$, an accepted offer buys $2 \times \tfrac{b}{2} = b$, exactly the price, so every offer breaks even. Below twice every offer loses; above twice the best offer is the most, £100m. The sign of $\tfrac{k}{2} - 1$ decides.

screens.title: Condition on winning
screens.prose:
Two curses, one rule: ask what winning tells you.

$$E[\text{overshoot}] = a\,\frac{n - 1}{n + 1}, \qquad E[\text{profit}] = \frac{b}{100}\left(\frac{kb}{2} - b\right)$$

The first comes from rival bidders, the second from a seller who knows more.
screens.question: For which values of k does any offer for the firm pay?

options.why: Above 1 the firm is worth more to you than to its owner, but you buy only the cheap ones. You need k above 2.

options.text: Any k, if the offer is small
options.why: A small offer still buys only firms worth less than it. The sign of $k/2 - 1$ is the same for every offer.

hints.text: Given acceptance the firm is worth $kb/2$ to you.
You pay $b$, so you gain when $k/2 > 1$.
k above 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $kb/2$ with the price $b$.

explain.text: An accepted offer buys a firm worth $kb/2$ to you for $b$. That pays only when $k > 2$. Below that, a seller's yes is bad news.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four questions, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Firm values are uniform from £0 to £100m, and the owner accepts any offer at least the value.

state.caption: The curve for a firm worth 3 times its value to you.

screens.question: Fill in the four answers.

rows: Ten bidders, errors ±£20: the winner's mean overshoot (£)
Four bidders, errors ±£12: the winner's mean overshoot (£)
Firm worth 1.8 times its value to you: the best offer (£m)
Firm worth 3 times: the expected profit of the best offer (£m)

hints.text: Use $a\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}$ and $\tfrac{b}{100}(\tfrac{kb}{2} - b)$.
1.8 is below 2, so every offer loses; 3 is above 2, so offer £100m.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r2c1: At 1.8 an accepted offer buys $0.9b$ for $b$, a loss. Offer nothing.
byKey.r3c1: At 3, offer £100m: always accepted, worth $3 \times 50 = 150$ for 100, so +£50m.

explain.text: Overshoots: $20 \times \tfrac{9}{11} = 16.36$ and $12 \times \tfrac35 = 7.20$. At 1.8 each accepted offer buys $0.9b$ for $b$, so offer nothing. At 3, offering £100m buys an average firm worth £150m: +£50m.

screens.title: Follow-up: what did you win
screens.prose: The interviewer says you won the jar among five bidders, errors ±£10, with an estimate of £100. You know nothing else about V.
screens.question: What is your best guess of V, in £?

hints.text: Winning means your error was the largest of five.
That error averages £6.67.

feedback.correct: About £93.33: take off the winner's mean overshoot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the winner's average error.

byKey.same: £100 is your estimate before you knew you won. Winning says it was the highest of five.
byKey.ten: £10 is the largest error possible. The winner's error averages £6.67.

explain.text: Winning means your estimate had the largest of five errors, which averages £6.67. So your best guess is $100 - 6.67 = £93.33$. A fill on your bid is a win too: `micro` l11-adverse-selection's adverse selection is the same curse.

ideas: When everyone estimates the same prize, the winning estimate is the highest, so it was probably too high.
With $n$ errors uniform on $\pm a$, the winner overshoots by $a\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}$ on average.
Facing a seller who knows the value, ask what it is worth given that your offer is accepted.

formula.name: Winner's curse
formula.note: Shade by this; it grows with the number of bidders.

summary.trap: Using the unconditional average. Condition on winning, or on the seller saying yes.

quiz.prose: Six bidders estimate a common value, each with an error uniform from −£14 to +£14, and each bids the estimate.
quiz.question: By how much does the winner overshoot on average, in £?

byKey.zero: Each error averages 0, but the winner's is the largest of six.

explain.text: The largest of six errors averages $14 \times \tfrac{5}{7} = £10$.

quiz.prose: A firm is worth V to its owner, uniform from £0 to £100m, and 1.2V to you. The owner accepts any offer at least V.
quiz.question: What is the expected profit of an offer of £50m, in £m?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on acceptance, then weight by its chance.

byKey.given: −20 is the loss once accepted. Weight it by the chance of acceptance, 0.5.
byKey.naive: That uses the average firm, £60m to you. Accepted firms average £25m, worth £30m.

explain.text: Accepted with chance 0.5, the firm then averages £25m, worth £30m to you. So $0.5 \times (30 - 50) = -£10$m.

quiz.prose: In a common-value auction, the number of rival bidders doubles.
quiz.question: How should you change your bid?

options.text: Shade more: winning now means beating more estimates
Shade less: more competition means bidding up
options.why: More bidders make the winning estimate more extreme, so the bad news in winning grows.

options.text: No change: your estimate is still unbiased
options.why: Your estimate is unbiased before the auction. Given that it wins, it is biased up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what winning against more rivals tells you.

explain.text: With more rivals, a winning estimate is the largest of more errors, so it overshoots by more. The overshoot $a\tfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}$ rises with $n$. So shade more.
